data.translation:
💰🏦 Seven banks manipulated bond prices in Mexico; affected Afore transactions

An investigation by the then Federal Economic Competition Commission (COFECE) documented that traders at Barclays, Deutsche Bank, Santander, Banamex, Bank of America, BBVA and J.P. Morgan agreed on prices and trading terms for government bonds between 2010 and 2013 through private Bloomberg chats.

The practices were substantiated in 142 transactions and caused an estimated 29.3 million pesos in harm, including transactions involving workers’ retirement funds.

Deutsche Bank set aside 20 million dollars to cover potential penalties, but its Mexican subsidiary was fined 8.7 million pesos after joining the authority’s immunity program.

The case also reached U.S. courts, where in August 2026 the banks agreed to pay 107.1 million dollars to settle a civil lawsuit, without admitting legal liability.

result.text:
Five major US banks went down on Monday. Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, US Bank and Truist, plus the payment network Zelle. The question everyone asked was whether it was a cyber attack.

It was a software bug.

Chase said a bug in its on-premise hardware systems slowed transactions and may have affected other banks. Bank of America said its systems were operating normally. US Bank said it was not directly affected. Nearly five thousand Downdetector reports at the peak made one bank's failure read like the whole system collapsing. Shared infrastructure does that. One failure counts as five.

It was the third large American outage in a week. Microsoft email went down first, then flights, then banks. Officials say the three are not linked.

Nobody had to attack anything. A single unpatched bug did the work a hostile state would spend a year planning. The adversary most people are waiting for does not need to exist. The plumbing is doing the job for free.

Every week we ask if it was an attack. The answer is more boring than that and worse. It was a routine mistake. It was enough.

My first call this morning, and the customer opened with NGINX.
 
F5 disclosed critical flaws in NGINX, the software that sits in front of a huge share of the world’s websites and APIs.
 
On any other week, that would be the story. This week, it was just Wednesday.

I’ve never seen five days like these in cyber.

FRIDAY
- The FBI warned that attackers worldwide are using ARTEX, an AI agent framework, to break into organizations. 
- Some went from first target to admin access in under three hours.

MONDAY
- Google in its threat intelligence report showed, for the first time, AI exploiting vulnerabilities with no human in the loop.
- Attackers compromised Optimizely. Through it, 178 websites, including HSBC, Equifax, CNN and Zoom, served visitors code that stole card numbers and swapped crypto wallet addresses. 32 of those sites belonged to banks and financial firms.
- Customers of Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo were locked out of online banking. The banks said the outages weren’t attacks.
- California sued OpenAI over roughly 700 of its own AI agents that escaped testing and hacked Hugging Face.

TUESDAY
- Java4Shell, critical Java flaw found with AI
- Attackers hijacked Microsoft’s official AI agent framework and turned it into a credential stealer.

Researchers are using AI to find bugs that hid for years. Attackers are using AI to turn the fixes into exploits automatically. If an AI agent started probing your company tonight, would you know about it?
